name: Colin Alvarez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Colin. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me both what you'd say in public and what you really think.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: No problem. I'm Colin, I'm 27, and I run the egg side of a mixed farm owned by the Pryce family. We've got sixteen thousand free-range laying hens in two sheds, and the rest of the farm is wheat and some beef.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Let's start simple. Walk me through a normal working day.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm in the first shed at five. I walk every row, check the water lines and the feed chain, pick up the eggs the hens have laid on the floor instead of in the nest boxes, and take out any dead birds. The conveyor brings the rest of the eggs to the packing room, and the lorry from the packing centre comes at eleven. Afternoons are paperwork, cleaning, and opening the pop holes so the hens go out on the range. I like it when it all runs smoothly, the sound of a calm shed. What wears me out is bird flu season, when we have to keep them indoors and everyone's on edge for months.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use any AI at the moment?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Now and then. I use a chat app to help write the monthly egg-quality report, and once to work out a treatment plan for red mite, which I then checked with the vet. My fiancée Jess works on reception at that same vet practice. We rent a place on the edge of town and we've got maybe three weeks of savings, which isn't much with a wedding planned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. We call this one AI Plateau.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fair enough. That sounds about right for most new things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a useful tool and nothing more, like the egg counter on the conveyor. Saves a bit of time, doesn't change who has to walk the sheds at five.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be fine with it. I'm not against the technology, but I wasn't counting on it either, and my job would look exactly the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the chat app for reports and keep doing the job. Jess and I would carry on saving for the wedding, which is June 2028 if we get there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like a quiet week with no bird flu warnings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any part of the work you'd actually like a machine to take?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Floor eggs, honestly. Every day there's two or three hundred of them, and I'm bent over picking them up for an hour. My back's twenty-seven going on sixty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much is the wedding going to cost?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About fifteen thousand all in, and we've got maybe a third. So it'd be overtime, the summer harvest on the arable side, and fewer takeaways.

S0.say: I'd say it's a useful tool and nothing more, like the egg counter on the conveyor. It saves a bit of time but someone still walks the sheds at five.
S0.think: I'd be fine with it, because I wasn't counting on it either way. My job would look exactly the same.
S0.do: Keeps using a chat app for monthly reports and carries on as normal. Saves for the June 2028 wedding through overtime on the arable harvest and fewer takeaways.
S0.feel: Calm, like a quiet week with no bird flu warnings.
S0.quote: Every day there's two or three hundred of them, and I'm bent over picking them up for an hour. My back's twenty-seven going on sixty.
S0.fieldNote: Colin is relaxed and practical, an occasional AI user who checks its advice with a vet. The one task he'd hand to a machine is picking up floor eggs, for his back's sake. A wedding sets his money horizon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. We call this one Steady Disruption.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That one I'd take seriously. It feels like the likely one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say adapt or get left behind, but in a calm way. I'd tell the lads at the feed merchant that the robots are coming for the boring jobs first, and that's not all bad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think egg units get robots that walk the sheds and pick up floor eggs, and cameras that spot sick birds. The Pryces could run both sheds with one person instead of two, and the other person is either me or Kevin, my assistant.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait until a farm nearby has had a shed robot for a full year, then I'd ask the Pryces to put me on the training. I'd start using the chat app properly for the flock records, not just the reports, so I'm the one who knows the data. I'd also bump our savings up, maybe forty a month extra.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like seeing the mortality numbers creep up a bit two days running.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned Kevin. Would you worry about him?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would. Kevin's fifty-two and he's been with the Pryces longer than I've been alive. But I'm engaged and he's got a pension coming, so it'd be a horrible, honest conversation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the wedding plan change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd keep it. We might make it smaller, fewer guests, but we'd keep the date.

S1.say: I'd say adapt or get left behind, but calmly. The robots come for the boring jobs first, and that's not all bad.
S1.think: I think shed robots and sick-bird cameras mean the Pryces can run both sheds with one person instead of two. The other person is either me or Kevin, my assistant.
S1.do: Waits for a nearby farm to run a shed robot for a full year, then asks his employer for training. Uses the chat app for flock records to become the person who knows the data, and saves about forty a month extra.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like mortality numbers creeping up two days running.
S1.quote: The Pryces could run both sheds with one person instead of two, and the other person is either me or Kevin, my assistant.
S1.fieldNote: He sees the job cut as a straight choice between himself and a colleague, and he is uncomfortable about it. His steady style shows in wanting a full year of proof on a neighbour's farm. The wedding goes ahead, only smaller.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. We call this one AGI by 2028.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2028? That's the year we're getting married.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need a plan from the government, and quickly, and I don't much care which party comes up with it. I'd say farm workers need help the same as office workers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think egg production would be one of the first to go fully robotic, because it's indoors and it's the same thing every day. I'd be out of a job about the same time I'm saying my vows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut everything that isn't rent and food, and we'd move the wedding to the registry office with twenty people. I'd start looking for work that robots can't easily reach, maybe with Jess's practice, maybe as a farm vet technician if they still need them. And I'd keep the Pryces' sheds running as long as they'd have me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, close to alarmed. It's the timing that gets me, not just the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would Jess feel about a smaller wedding?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say it's just a party, we'd still be married. She's better at this than I am.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame, if anyone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nobody in particular. The companies are doing what companies do. The government should have seen it coming, but I don't think any of them really did.

S2.say: I'd say we need a plan from the government quickly, and I don't much care which party makes it. Farm workers need help the same as office workers.
S2.think: I think egg production goes robotic first because it's indoors and the same every day. I'd be out of a job about the time I'm saying my vows.
S2.do: Cuts everything but rent and food and moves the wedding to a registry office with twenty guests. Looks for work at Jess's vet practice or as a farm vet technician while keeping the sheds running as long as he's needed.
S2.feel: Anxious, close to alarmed, mostly because of the timing with the wedding.
S2.quote: I'd be out of a job about the same time I'm saying my vows.
S2.fieldNote: The two-year date lands on his wedding year, which makes the scenario personal at once. He blames no one and calls government planning the real gap. He reaches for his fiancée's workplace as the safest nearby option.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. We call this one AGI by 2031.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Okay, that's after the wedding at least.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to adjust if we start now. I'd push the Pryces to train their staff rather than just buy the robots and lay people off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think five years is about right for me. I'm not a jumper, but I'm not a stick-in-the-mud either. Give me two years to watch and three to move, and I'll be fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For the first two years I'd learn every bit of kit that comes into the sheds and keep saving. In year three, I'd do the vet technician course part-time, so I've got something if the sheds go fully robot. I'd want us to have a small pot, maybe three months of money, by the time it lands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Manageable. More like a to-do list than a fright.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if you train and then the robots do vet technician work too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd still have a skill that's about animals rather than about sheds. Sick birds and sick cows still need someone to notice, at least for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does five years change any family plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd probably wait to have kids until after 2031, to see where we land. Jess wants them sooner, so that one's still under discussion.

S3.say: I'd say there's time to adjust if we start now. I'd push the Pryces to train their staff rather than just buy robots and lay people off.
S3.think: Five years is about right for me. Give me two years to watch and three to move, and I'll be fine.
S3.do: Learns every new piece of shed kit for two years while saving, then takes a part-time vet technician course in year three. Aims for about three months of savings by 2031 and may delay children.
S3.feel: Uneasy but manageable, more like a to-do list than a fright.
S3.quote: Give me two years to watch and three to move, and I'll be fine.
S3.fieldNote: Five years fits his steady style exactly: watch first, then move. He builds his backup plan on caring for animals, which he sees as harder to replace. He and his fiancée disagree about the timing of children, which he admitted plainly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. We call this one AGI by 2036.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's a proper amount of time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's no reason anyone should be caught out. Companies should train people, the government should help pay for it, and people like me should actually turn up to the courses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years is so long that I might get lazy. But I've watched the farm change a lot in nine years already, so I don't think I'd sit still.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going in the sheds and save steadily. Around year five, I'd do the vet technician course, or maybe a course in fixing the farm robots, whichever has more jobs by then. We'd have kids in that decade, probably sooner rather than later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit of background worry, but nothing that keeps me up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How has the farm changed in the nine years you've been there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When I started, we collected every egg by hand. Now the conveyor does it and I just do the floor ones. That's the change already, it just happened slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you still worry about in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kevin, mostly. Ten years takes him to sixty-two. He'd need a bridge to his pension, not a course.

S4.say: I'd say nobody should be caught out with this much notice. Companies should train people, the government should help pay, and people like me should actually turn up.
S4.think: Ten years is so long I might get lazy. But I've watched the farm change a lot in nine years already, so I don't think I'd sit still.
S4.do: Keeps working the sheds and saves steadily, then around year five takes either a vet technician course or a farm robot repair course, whichever has more jobs. Plans to have children with Jess within the decade.
S4.feel: Mostly calm, with a little background worry.
S4.quote: He'd need a bridge to his pension, not a course.
S4.fieldNote: He points to the egg conveyor as proof that big change can arrive slowly without much harm. His worry moves to an older colleague who needs a route to his pension, not retraining. In this picture his family plans go ahead.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because it lands on our wedding and we'd have nothing saved. What would help is the government paying for short courses for farm workers, and some kind of bridge for older workers like Kevin to reach their pension.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Bird flu, actually. People forget farming already has shocks. We get through those because the vets and the government step in. It would be good if AI had the same kind of plan.

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Thanks. I'll tell Jess I was interviewed, she'll think it's funny.

headlineQuote: I'd be out of a job about the same time I'm saying my vows.
portrait: Colin is a 27-year-old egg unit manager on a mixed farm, engaged to Jess, who works at the local vet practice, with about three weeks of savings and a wedding set for June 2028. He uses AI tools now and then and checks their advice with experts, and he's pragmatic about change rather than for or against it. Under gradual change he waits for proof, then trains. The two-year picture alarms him because it lands on his wedding year. With five or ten years he calmly plans a move into vet technician work while worrying for an older colleague near retirement.
biggestWorry: The two-year AGI scenario, because it lands on his wedding year and he and Jess would have nothing saved.
whatWouldHelp: Government-funded short courses for farm workers, and a bridge to retirement for older workers like his colleague Kevin.
